faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Newton garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. At Newton's edges the gardens back onto pasture and brush, and the groundhog den sits in that brush line with a worn path to the beds. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Newton.wildlife_intro:
Newton is Sussex County's seat, a hilltop town of Victorian and colonial homes around Spring Street, older neighborhoods climbing the slopes, and farmland and woods starting at the town line in every direction. The Paulins Kill runs below the town. Raccoons and bats work the older homes near the center, groundhogs and skunks take the edge lots, squirrels are constant in the street trees, and the surrounding ridges hold copperhead and rattlesnake country that Newton residents live alongside carefully. It is a small town with a full rural animal roster.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Newton's chimneys are old brick on old houses, and the cap, crown, and flashing check is part of every inspection here, not a specialty referral.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Sparta Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. Lake Mohawk's chimneys stand cold for weeks between visits, which is precisely what a spring raccoon mother is looking for, and the fitted cap is the lake house's best single purchase. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

faqs.q: I found a snake in my Sparta Township yard — could it be venomous?
faqs.a: Possibly, in this part of New Jersey, which is why identification comes before everything. The northern copperhead (state-Threatened) favors rocky, wooded slopes here, and the timber rattlesnake (state-Endangered) holds on along the ridges; both are left strictly alone and referred to NJ Fish & Wildlife's Venomous Snake Response Team. Sparta's rocky ridges and sunny ledges are within the ranges of both of the state's venomous snakes, so a heavy-banded snake here is photographed, identified, and left for the specialists if it is one of them. Most calls turn out to be harmless black rat snakes or garter snakes, which we can catch and release outdoors within 200 meters, as state policy allows.

Sparta Township.wildlife_intro:
Sparta pairs a famous lake community with a growing township: Lake Mohawk's alpine-styled cottages and year-round homes around its boardwalk lake, Sparta Lake, and newer subdivisions spreading along the township's ridges and valleys. The lake homes sit empty in stretches and under heavy woods, prime conditions for raccoons in chimneys and bats in cottage attics. Groundhogs dig the clearings, skunks work the lawns, squirrels are everywhere the oaks are, and the rocky township woods are snake country where identification matters.

Empty houses invite quiet tenants. A home closed for the winter gives raccoons and bats months of undisturbed tenure, and the damage is usually discovered in a single bad hour at spring opening: fouled insulation, stained ceilings, a chimney full of nesting. Pre-closing walk-throughs in the fall — caps checked, vents screened, gaps at the waterline and roofline sealed — cost far less than post-winter remediation. For owners who are away, a neighbor or caretaker holding a key is the next best thing; small leaks and small entries both grow in an empty house. Lake Mohawk's calendar is the inspection calendar here: the fall closing check and the spring opening survey catch what the empty months would otherwise hide.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Vernon Township porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Vernon Township with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Vernon Township homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Vernon Township host summer colonies, and in Sussex County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.

Vernon Township gives our crew a Sussex mix shaped by Lake Mohawk and the county's glacial lakes and the housing around it. Bats and raccoons in lake homes around Mohawk, Hopatcong and Culver are the summer staple, groundhogs work the farm valleys around Newton and Wantage, and the Kittatinny Ridge holds the state's best-known timber rattlesnake country — state-Endangered, strictly referral — and Vernon Township is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Newton, Franklin and Sussex Borough keep older mill and mining-town stock, Sparta and Vernon hold lake cottages and ski-area condos and homes, and the valleys are farmhouses and rural homes on large wooded lots. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Vernon Township; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Vernon Township jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: A bat got into my living room in Hopatcong — what should I do?
faqs.a: Close the bat in one room, open a window or exterior door in that room, turn off the lights, and let it leave on its own at dusk; never handle it bare-handed. In a Hopatcong cottage a bat in the bedroom in August usually means the colony is in the roof void overhead, and the visit becomes a full cottage survey, with the living spaces sealed off from the roost the same day. If anyone slept in the room or a pet made contact, call your local health department — they decide whether the bat should be tested. A single bat usually means a gap worth finding, and we can check the rooflines and vents that let it in.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Hopatcong porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Hopatcong decks stairstep down wooded slopes, and the voids beneath them are skunk and groundhog housing with a lake view; screening them follows the slope, not the deck's rectangle. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

Hopatcong.wildlife_intro:
Hopatcong is the borough on the big lake's western shore: steep, wooded streets of former summer cottages, many converted to year-round homes in stages, plus newer houses on the heights. The cottages' layered additions and low attics are animal architecture. Raccoons den in the chimneys and under the decks, bats hold the cottage attics through the summer season, squirrels commute from the heavy woods, skunks work the shore lawns, and water snakes along the docks get reported as something more sinister every July. Empty weekdays are the animals' opportunity.

Waterfront houses fight moisture on every front. Crawlspaces on pilings, bulkhead walls, and dock structures give raccoons and opossums dry travel lanes straight to the floor system, and salt air eats vent screens and fasteners years faster than it does inland. Materials matter here: stainless and heavy-gauge mesh, sealed penetrations where pipes pass through the foundation, and caps that survive storm wind. Bats favor the warm, still air under raised houses and inside their roof voids. A shore house proofed with inland materials is a shore house scheduled for a second visit. Hopatcong's shore cottages take lake weather full in the face, so caps, screens, and fasteners here are specified for wind and wet, and the deck voids over the slope get the deepest screening.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Franklin attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. Franklin callers in June usually have a maternity colony overhead, and the honest plan here is documented, dated, and patient: survey now, exclusion when the guideline window opens in August. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for wildlife work in Franklin?
faqs.a: Budget for three parts rather than one: getting the animals out, closing every entry they used, and cleaning what they left. The Franklin budget turns on colony age: a first-year roost is a sealing job, while a decade of guano in a low mining-era attic adds a cleanup that has to be priced from photographs, not optimism. Skipping the second part is the classic false economy — a cheap removal with open entries is usually a second removal by the next season, and the written quote separates the parts so you can see that plainly.

Franklin.wildlife_intro:
Franklin, the Sussex County borough, is the old zinc-mining town in the Wallkill valley: modest older homes on the hillside streets, the Franklin Mineral Museum, and mine-scarred, rocky ground around it. Bats are part of the town's underground story, the region's old mines are hibernation country, and the attics of Franklin's older homes hold summer colonies most years. Raccoons work the chimneys, groundhogs dig the rocky lots where they can, skunks make their rounds, and rats appear around the older commercial blocks on Main Street.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Franklin attic jobs start with a colony history, because in mine country the same houses host bats decade after decade, and the guano layers usually prove it.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Sussex Borough lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. Sussex Borough lawns sit over rich valley soil at the farm ring's edge, and the cone-holing appears first on the streets closest to the fields, where the grubs and the skunks both commute in from. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

faqs.q: I can hear baby animals in my Sussex Borough wall — can you just seal the hole?
faqs.a: Not yet, and any company offering to should worry you. Sealing a mother out with a litter inside converts a removal into dead animals in the wall. Spring chirping in a Sussex Borough chimney usually means a raccoon litter over the damper, and the flue camera comes before any discussion of caps or timing. We locate the litter first, then time the work so the family leaves or is taken out together — one-way exits sized for the species, or hands-on removal where the young cannot climb. The hole gets sealed the same visit the last animal is confirmed out, not before.

Sussex Borough.wildlife_intro:
Sussex Borough is a one-square-mile old town in the Clove valley, completely ringed by Wantage Township farms: a Main Street of older homes and small businesses, side streets of Victorians and capes, and Clove Brook running through. The farm ring means the borough's wildlife is farm wildlife on a town schedule. Groundhogs dig in from the field edges, raccoons den in the borough chimneys, bats hold the older attics, skunks make nightly rounds of the whole town, and squirrels work the street trees. Nothing here is far from a field.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Sussex Borough yards end at working farmland in most directions, so the burrow survey here includes the fence line and the first yards of field beyond it.
